'''Charles Max Stein''' (March 22, 1920 &ndash; November 24, 2016) was an American mathematical statistician and professor of [[statistics]] at [[Stanford University]].

He received his Ph.D. in 1947 at [[Columbia University]] with advisor [[Abraham Wald]]. He held faculty positions at [[University of California at Berkeley|Berkeley]] and the [[University of Chicago]] before moving permanently to Stanford in 1953. He is known for [[Stein's paradox]] in [[decision theory]], which shows that [[ordinary least squares]] estimates can be uniformly improved when many parameters are estimated;<ref>{{cite journal|title=Special Section: Minimax Shrinkage Estimation: A Tribute to Charles Stein|journal=Statistical Science|date=February 2012|volume=27|issue=1|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ss/1331729974#toc}}</ref> for [[Stein's lemma]], giving a formula for the [[covariance]] of one [[random variable]] with the value of a function of another when the two random variables are [[joint normal distribution|jointly normally distributed]]; for the [[Error exponents in hypothesis testing#Optimal error exponent for Neyman–Pearson testing|Chernoff-Stein Lemma]]<ref>{{cite book 
|last1=Cover 
|first1=Thomas M. 
|last2=Thomas 
|first2=Joy A. 
|title=Elements of information theory 
|date=2006 
|publisher=Wiley-Interscience 
|location=Hoboken, N.J 
|isbn=9780471241959 
|edition=2nd }}</ref> which states that the [[Kullback Leibler divergence]] describes the optimal [[Type I and type II errors|type II error]] exponent for the [[Neyman–Pearson lemma|Neyman-Pearson]] setting in hypothesis testing, and for [[Stein's method]], a way of proving theorems such as the [[Central Limit Theorem]] that does not require the variables to be independent and identically distributed.<ref>{{cite journal|title=A bound for the error in the normal approximation to the distribution of a sum of dependent random variables| url=http://digitalassets.lib.berkeley.edu/math/ucb/text/math_s6_v2_article-34.pdf}}</ref> He was a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]. He died in November 2016 at the age of 96.<ref>{{cite news|title=Charles M. Stein, extraordinary statistician and anti-war activist, dies at 96|url=http://news.stanford.edu/2016/12/01/charles-m-stein-extraordinary-statistician-anti-war-activist-dies-96/|publisher=Stanford News Service|date=December 1, 2016}}</ref>

==Works==
*''Approximate Computation of Expectations'', Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Hayward, CA, 1986.
* A bound for the error in the normal approximation to the distribution of a sum of dependent random variables, Sixth Berkeley Stanford Symposium, pages 583–602.
